# Block 1: AI-assisted R programming {.unnumbered} ## Prerequisites - A GitHub account, an IDE (RStudio or Positron), and the Git, `renv` and `testthat` skills from earlier sessions. - **Claude Code**, the workshop's main tool, installed and checked before the day: follow [Setting up Claude Code](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd). It needs a Claude Pro, Max, Teams or Enterprise seat, or a Console account. - **Posit Assistant** works as an alternative; each page says where it differs. - **GitHub Copilot** (Copilot Free is enough) for the inline completions in Block 2. - Your institution's permission to use these tools, and, near research data, your ethics approval and data agreements. Block 4 covers this. ## Learning outcomes By the end of the day you will be able to: 1. Explain what a large language model is and why the model choice matters. 2. Use inline completion and know what context it sees. 3. Debug your own code with AI, and know when AI helps most. 4. Choose how much an agent may do, and know every route by which your data leave your machine. 5. Write an `AGENTS.md` instruction file and a skill, and test that they load. 6. Protect files with a permission rule, and detect any change with git. 7. Have an agent clean data against a codebook you own, and check it with tests. 8. Use AI as a code reviewer, and grade it against a known answer. 9. Have an agent refactor code under a characterisation testA test that checks new code reproduces the saved output of the original code exactly. It shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct., with the reference in your hands. 10. Check an AI translation, report results without typed numbers, and leave with a documented, tested repository. ## The day at a glance Times are approximate. | Time | Session | |---|---| | 09:00 | Block 1: AI-assisted R programming | | 09:15 | Blocks 2–3: Inline completions; Debugging with AI | | 10:00 | Block 4: Context, disclosure and autonomy | | 10:35 | Break | | 10:50 | Block 5: Instructions and skills | | 11:35 | Block 6: Enforced controls | | 12:05 | Lunch | | 13:05 | Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI | | 13:55 | Block 8: AI-assisted code review | | 14:35 | Break | | 14:50 | Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged | | 15:25 | Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results | | 15:55 | Wrap-up: run the whole test suite | | 16:00 | Close | Every block ends with a *Going further* section that is not covered live. ## Materials You work in your own copy of a workshop template repository ([its layout](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#your-workshop-repository)), forked before the day. It holds a synthetic voles dataset, scripts, and three things that make the day forgiving: - **Tests that wait.** Each test in `tests/` skips until its block is done; at 16:00 they run together as one suite. - **Checkpoint branches.** `block5-done`, `block7-done` and `block9-done`: if you fall behind, switch to the next one from the Git pane's branch menu and carry on. Nobody needs to finish every exercise. - **Built-in protections.** The raw data, the checks and the references are protected before you start. Block 8 also uses the project folder from that you reviewed on Day 2. **Verification is the workshop's only non-negotiable**, and it is what lets you automate with confidence: once you can check an agent's work quickly and independently, you can hand it more of the work. Every exercise ends with that check. ## The thread through the day: Check · Reproduce · Record Every block applies three habits, and ends with a box saying what it added: - **Check.** Treat what an AI produces as a claim, and verify it independently: the data, a test, a reference you hold, the Git pane's diff, or your own knowledge of the biology. - **Reproduce.** The code runs in a fresh R sessionAn R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with “never save .RData” set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record. with the package versions in the lockfileThe renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment., and nothing changed that you did not see. - **Record.** Leave the evidence a reader needs: a codebook, logs of every data change, numbers computed in code, and a log of your AI use, all drawn together in a README. ::::::: {.dia .dia-flow role="figure" aria-label="Files that accumulate in your workshop repository through the day: Block 4 adds the AI-use log; Block 5 adds your edits to AGENTS.md and a skill; Block 6 tests the shipped settings file; Block 7 adds the codebook and cleaning and exclusion logs; Block 9 adds the reference and tests; Block 10 adds a README that draws on all of them."} ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} **Block 4** `docs/ai-log.md` ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} **Block 5** `AGENTS.md` and a skill ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} **Block 6** `settings.json` in `.claude/`, read and tested ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} **Block 7** codebook, cleaning and exclusion logs ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} **Block 9** reference and tests ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-check} **Block 10** `README.md`, drawing on all of them ::: ::: {.dia-caption} What your repository holds by 16:00. ::: ::::::: **Your AI-use log.** From Block 4, after each block in which an agent does work, you add one line yourself to `docs/ai-log.md`. In Block 10 this AI-use logA record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README. becomes your README's AI declaration. Each line has this form: ``` date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed ``` ## Claude Code quick reference {#cc-quick-reference} Keep this open during the day. Everything in the right-hand column is typed at the Claude Code prompt unless it says otherwise ([where am I typing?](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#where-am-i-typing)). | To... | Type this | |---|---| | Start Claude Code in your workshop repository | Open the project in RStudio or Positron, then `claude` in its Terminal tab | | Ask for a plan before anything changes | `/plan` followed by your request, e.g. `/plan add a mass_change_g column` | | Approve a plan it has made | Choose **"Yes, manually approve edits"**, so it still asks before each change; "No, keep planning" to change the plan first | | See or add permission rules | `/permissions` | | Open your instruction file | `/memory`, then choose `AGENTS.md` | | List the skills it can use | `/skills` | | Start a new conversation, with nothing from the last one | `/clear` | | See which model it is using, for your AI-use log | It is shown above the prompt; `/model` opens a picker | | Check your privacy settings (Pro and Max accounts) | `/privacy-settings` | | Stop it while it is working | `Ctrl+C` | | Leave | `/exit` | | Change how much it may do without asking | `Shift+Tab` cycles the modes: Manual (`default`) → `acceptEdits` → `plan`, and `auto` where available | | Run one shell command without leaving it | Start the line with `!`. The output is added to the conversation, so it reaches the model | | Check its work while it runs | Use the R console and the Git pane, not the Terminal tab Claude Code is using: see [checking work](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#checking-work) | Your workshop repository starts Claude Code in **Manual** mode (`default`): it asks before every edit and command. Claude Code's own default is `auto`, where a second model approves actions for you; [Block 4](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd) explains the difference. Stay in Manual and read each request before you answer. ## Framing and mental models *⏱ ~15 minutes: presentation, a short discussion and a quiz.* Two words recur all day. An assistantAny AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course “assistant” is the general word; “agent” is used when the tool acts on your files. is any AI tool that helps you write or understand code. An agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises. is an assistant that acts: it reads your project and, if you let it, edits files and runs commands. Claude Code and Posit Assistant are agents; a chat window that only answers is not. ## What is a large language model? A large language model predicts the next fragment of text from what came before, having learnt from a large share of the public internet, code included. Every tool today is built on one. Models differ in code quality and in how often they invent functions that do not exist, so if a model gives you consistently poor suggestions and your plan lets you switch, switching is a cheap experiment. ## Why the context window matters An LLM has no memory between calls: each one starts with only what you supply, up to the limit of its context windowThe maximum amount of text a language model can consider in one call. The model has no memory between calls, so it sees only what is in the context window.. That one fact explains the day. Instruction files and skills give the model context it would not otherwise have; because they are only requests, Block 6 adds controls that hold either way, and tests check the result. **Remember:** the AI sees only what you give it, and everything it sees has left your machine. ## Discussion Take three minutes, then post a short answer to each question in the Zoom chat: 1. What is one task you would like to hand to an agent by 16:00, and how would you check it? Is there anything you would not delegate at all? 2. How do you use AI tools now: browser chat, IDE chat, a terminal agent? ## Check your understanding **Which statement best describes the difference between a local agent such as Claude Code and an asynchronous cloud agent?**
**True or false: a large language model has no memory between calls, so each interaction starts with only the context you supply.** ## Going further (not covered live) This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you. ### Which tool does what - **Claude Code** runs in the Terminal tab of RStudio or Positron, which starts in your project's root folder: the folder it acts on. Every block's main text uses it, and checks its work from the R console and Git pane. - **Posit Assistant** is the in-IDE chat and agent in RStudio and Positron. It can also see your live R session. See [What's new in Posit AI](https://docs.posit.co/posit-ai/whats-new/). - **GitHub Copilot** gives inline completions in all three IDEs. Its cloud agent, used only in some *Going further* sections, needs a paid plan; see the [Copilot plans page](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/get-started/plans). ### Models Claude Code uses Anthropic's Claude models; Posit Assistant runs on Posit AI or a provider key you configure; GitHub Copilot offers Claude, GPT and Gemini models. You do not need strong opinions about which model is best, only to know that the choice exists and changes the output. ### Two modes of execution The tools you use today are **synchronous and local**: they work on your machine, respond in seconds, and can be interrupted. Their reach differs: the current file for inline completion, the project folder and the output of its own commands for Claude Code, and your live R session too for Posit Assistant. An **asynchronous, remote** agent, such as the Copilot cloud agent, works on its own branch on someone else's servers and returns a pull request minutes later; you meet it in the *Going further* sections of Blocks 4, 6 and 9. The first invites you to watch and interrupt; the second, to write a precise specification and review what comes back. Block 4 turns this into a ladder of autonomy. ### The thread, in more detail Day 1 introduced `renv`; Day 4 checks that an agent has kept to it. On Day 2 you saw what a reviewable project needs ([TADA! and the README](06-reproducibility.qmd#repro-fix), and [the SORTEE checklist](06-reproducibility.qmd#repro-sortee)); Day 4 shows how AI can help produce that record without inventing any of it. Many journals, funders and institutions now ask authors to declare AI use, and a log written at the time is easier and more accurate than one reconstructed later. ## Glossary ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
term definition
agent An assistant that can read across a project's files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.
AI-use log A record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.
assistant Any AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course "assistant" is the general word; "agent" is used when the tool acts on your files.
characterisation test A test that checks new code reproduces the saved output of the original code exactly. It shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct.
context window The maximum amount of text a language model can consider in one call. The model has no memory between calls, so it sees only what is in the context window.
fresh R session An R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with "never save .RData" set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record.
lockfile The renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.
````` ::: :::
